topics.title: P1.1 What are the risks and benefits of using radiations?

outcomes.text: Name the groups of the electromagnetic spectrum from radio to gamma and how wavelength, frequency and energy change across it.
Recall that our eyes detect only a small range of frequencies.
Recall that all electromagnetic radiation travels through space at the same very high, finite speed.
Explain with examples that electromagnetic radiation transfers energy from source to absorber.
Recall that substances absorb, transmit or reflect radiation in ways that depend on wavelength.
Recall that electron arrangements in atoms change when radiation is absorbed or emitted, and that atoms can become ions by losing outer electrons.
Recall which changes in molecules, atoms and nuclei generate and absorb radiations: gamma from nuclei, X-rays and visible from electrons, ionisation, ozone, infrared in molecules.
Describe the hazardous effects of ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays, notably on human tissue.
Give practical uses of radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma radiation.
Recall that radio waves are produced by, or can induce, oscillations in electrical circuits.

topics.title: P1.2 What is climate change and what is the evidence for it?

subtopics.title: Radiation balance and the greenhouse effect

outcomes.text: Explain that all bodies emit radiation whose intensity and wavelength distribution depend on temperature.
Explain how a body's temperature depends on the balance of incoming, absorbed and emitted radiation, with everyday examples and factors that set the Earth's temperature.

topics.title: P1.3 How do waves behave?

outcomes.text: Describe wave motion using amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period.
Describe evidence that for water ripples and sound in air it is the wave, not the medium, that travels.
Describe transverse and longitudinal waves, with waves on a rope and sound in air as examples.
Define wavelength and frequency.
Recall and apply wave speed = frequency x wavelength.
Describe how to measure the speed of water ripples and of sound in air, including with a ripple tank.
Describe the effects of reflection and refraction at material interfaces, including measuring refraction through a prism and reflection from a plane mirror.
Recall that wave speed differs between substances and may vary with wavelength.
Explain refraction as a change in wave speed, which changes wavelength and may change direction.
Recall that light is an electromagnetic wave and that electromagnetic waves are transverse.

topics.title: P1.4 What happens when light and sound meet different materials? (separate science only)

outcomes.text: Construct and interpret ray diagrams showing specular reflection by mirrors.
Construct and interpret ray diagrams for refraction at a plane surface and dispersion by a prism.
Use ray diagrams to compare convex and concave lenses.
Describe transmission and absorption of waves at material interfaces.
Explain how colour relates to differential absorption, transmission and scattering.
Describe examples of sound being transmitted through solids.
Explain that sound transmission through ear bones works over a limited frequency range and why that matters for hearing.
Explain how differences in speed, absorption and reflection of waves in solids and liquids are used to detect hidden structures: ultrasound imaging, earthquake waves and SONAR.
Show how speed, frequency and wavelength change together when sound passes between media.

topics.title: P2.1 How much energy do we use?

outcomes.text: Describe how energy in chemical stores is transferred by an electric current doing work on domestic devices.
Explain how appliance power ratings, time in use and changes in stored energy are related.
Recall and apply energy transferred = power x time, in joules or kilowatt-hours.
Describe with examples energy transfers in a system, with no net change in total energy of a closed system.
Describe examples of dissipation, where energy ends up stored in less useful ways.
Explain ways to reduce unwanted energy transfer, such as lubrication and thermal insulation.
Describe how wall thickness and thermal conductivity affect a building's rate of cooling.
Recall and apply efficiency = useful energy transferred / total energy transferred, and describe ways to raise efficiency.
Interpret and construct Sankey diagrams showing that energy is conserved.

topics.title: P2.2 How can electricity be generated?

outcomes.text: Describe the main energy resources on Earth: fossil fuels, nuclear fuel, biofuel, wind, hydroelectricity, tides and the Sun.
Explain the differences between renewable and non-renewable resources.
Compare how the main energy resources are used to generate electricity.
Explain patterns and trends in energy resource use in domestic, workplace and national contexts.

subtopics.title: Mains electricity and the National Grid

outcomes.text: Recall that UK mains is a.c. at 50 Hz and about 230 V, and explain the difference between direct and alternating voltage.
Recall that transformers raise voltage for transmission across the National Grid and lower it for local domestic use.
Recall the functions of live, neutral and earth wires and explain why a live wire can be dangerous even with a switch open.

topics.title: P3.1 What is electric charge? (separate science only)

outcomes.text: Describe how rubbing produces static electricity and sparks, and the evidence that charged objects attract or repel without touching, weakening with distance.
Explain how transfer of electrons between objects causes static electricity.
Explain the electric field and how it helps explain static electricity.

topics.title: P3.2 What determines the current in an electric circuit?

outcomes.text: Recall that current is the rate of flow of charge, needing a source of potential difference and a closed circuit, and is the same at every point in a single loop.
Recall and use charge = current x time.
Recall that current depends on resistance and potential difference, and the units of each.
Recall and apply V = I x R in d.c. series circuits, and describe an experiment to investigate the resistance of a wire.
Recall that some components have constant resistance while others, like heating elements and lamp filaments, change as current changes.
Use graphs to decide whether circuit elements are linear or non-linear and relate the curves to their function.
Describe experiments to find I-V characteristics of lamps, diodes, LDRs and thermistors, with circuit diagrams.
Represent circuits using correct terminal conventions and symbols for lamps, diodes, LDRs, thermistors, switches and fixed and variable resistors.

topics.title: P3.3 How do series and parallel circuits work?

outcomes.text: Relate potential difference to the work done on or by a given amount of charge: V = energy transferred / charge.
Describe the differences between series and parallel circuits, including how current and potential difference change when a component's resistance changes, and how to investigate bulb brightness.
Explain why two resistors in series increase net resistance while two in parallel decrease it.
Solve problems for series circuits using equivalent resistance.
Explain the design and use of d.c. series circuits for measurement and testing, including the effect of changing current, light on an LDR and temperature on an NTC thermistor.

topics.title: P3.4 What determines the rate of energy transfer in a circuit?

outcomes.text: Describe the energy transfers when a current flows through a component.
Explain how a device's power relates to energy transferred over time: P = E / t.
Recall and use energy transferred = charge x potential difference.
Recall and apply P = V x I and P = I squared x R.
Use conservation of energy to show that a transformer stepping up voltage lowers the current, using Vp x Ip = Vs x Is.
Explain why transmitting power at higher voltage is more efficient.

topics.title: P3.5 What are magnetic fields?

outcomes.text: Describe attraction and repulsion between like and unlike poles of permanent magnets.
Describe a magnet's field and how its strength and direction vary from point to point.
Explain how a compass behaves and why this is evidence that the Earth's core is magnetic.
Distinguish permanent from induced magnets.
Describe how to show that a current creates a magnetic effect.
Describe the pattern and directions of the magnetic field around a current-carrying wire.
Recall that field strength depends on the current and distance from the conductor.
Explain how a solenoid's magnetic effect can be increased.
Explain how a solenoid generates sound in loudspeakers and headphones (separate science only).

topics.title: P3.6 How do electric motors work?

outcomes.text: Describe the interaction forces between a magnet and a current-carrying conductor in terms of magnetic fields.
Use Fleming's left-hand rule to relate force, conductor and field orientations.
Apply force = magnetic flux density x current x length of conductor.
Explain how the force on a conductor in a magnetic field turns a rectangular coil in a simple electric motor.

topics.title: P3.7 What is the process inside an electric generator? (separate science only)

outcomes.text: Recall that a changing magnetic field around a conductor can induce a potential difference that drives a current.
Explain how a moving coil microphone turns sound pressure variations into varying current.
Recall that the induced current produces a field opposing the original change.
Explain a potential difference-time graph for an alternator producing a.c.
Explain how an alternator is adapted into a dynamo producing d.c.
Explain how an alternating current in one coil induces a current in another, as in transformers.
Describe how the ratio of potential differences across a transformer's coils depends on the ratio of turns.
Apply transformer equations for potential difference, turns, current and power, and relate them to the advantages of high-voltage transmission.

topics.title: P4.1 What are forces?

subtopics.title: Interaction pairs and Newton's third law

outcomes.text: Recall and apply Newton's third law: interaction pairs are equal, opposite and act on different objects.
Recall interactions by gravity, electrostatics, magnetism and contact (normal force and friction), and describe how each involves a pair of objects.
Represent interaction forces as vectors.
Define weight and describe how it is measured.
Recall and apply weight = mass x gravitational field strength.

topics.title: P4.2 How can we describe motion?

outcomes.text: Recall and apply average speed = distance / time.
Recall typical everyday speeds for wind, sound, walking, running, cycling and transport.
Measure distances and times to calculate speeds, including investigating a trolley down a ramp.
Convert units using ratios, including between m/s and km/h.
Explain the vector-scalar distinction: displacement and distance, velocity and speed.
Recall and apply acceleration = change in speed / time and describe how to investigate acceleration.
Select and apply (final speed) squared minus (initial speed) squared = 2 x acceleration x distance.
Recall the acceleration in free fall and estimate everyday accelerations.
Draw and use distance-time and speed-time graphs to find speeds and accelerations.
Interpret lines and slopes of distance-time and velocity-time graphs.
Interpret enclosed areas in velocity-time graphs.

topics.title: P4.3 What is the connection between forces and motion?

outcomes.text: Describe forces acting on an isolated object or system.
Use free body diagrams to show how several forces give a resultant, including balanced forces.
Use scale vector diagrams to add forces (parallel and perpendicular only).
Recall and apply momentum = mass x velocity and the conservation of momentum in collisions.
Apply Newton's second law: change in momentum = resultant force x time.
Apply Newton's first law to uniform motion and to motion where speed or direction changes.
Explain that circular orbital motion has constant speed but changing velocity.
Explain inertial mass as force over acceleration.
Recall and apply force = mass x acceleration.
Use equations linking force, mass, velocity, acceleration and momentum to explain relationships.
Describe examples where forces cause rotation.
Define and calculate the moment of a force = force x perpendicular distance.
Explain how levers and gears transmit rotational effects.
Explain methods of measuring human reaction times and recall typical results.
Explain the factors affecting emergency stopping distance and the safety implications.
Explain the dangers of large decelerations and estimate forces on a public road.
Estimate stopping distances over typical speeds from data (separate science only).
Use estimates of speeds, times and masses to calculate large accelerations and forces in road transport (separate science only).

topics.title: P4.4 How can we describe motion in terms of energy transfers? (separate science only)

outcomes.text: Describe the energy transfers when forces do work, such as raising an object or moving it along the line of the force.
Recall and apply work done = force x distance.
Calculate kinetic energy = half x mass x speed squared.
Calculate gravitational potential energy = mass x gravitational field strength x height.
Calculate energy transfers for mechanical processes and convert between newton metres and joules.
Describe how energy is stored as systems change: projectile, impact, constant force, braking vehicle.
Explain power as the rate of energy transfer.
Recall and apply power = energy transferred / time.

topics.title: P5.1 What is radioactivity?

outcomes.text: Describe the atom as a positive nucleus surrounded by electrons, with a tiny nucleus holding almost all the mass.
Describe how the atomic model changed through Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford and Bohr.
Recall the typical size of atoms and small molecules.
Recall that nuclei hold protons and neutrons, and that each element has a characteristic nuclear charge.
Explain isotopes and show them with conventional notation.
Recall that unstable nuclei may emit alpha, beta, neutrons or gamma radiation.
Relate each emission to changes in the mass or charge of the nucleus.
Write balanced nuclear equations for alpha, beta, gamma and neutron emission.
Explain half-life and its link to the random nature of decay.
Calculate the net decline in emission after a whole number of half-lives.
Interpret activity-time graphs to find half-life.

topics.title: P5.2 How can radioactive materials be used safely?

outcomes.text: Recall the differing penetration of alpha, beta and gamma radiation.
Distinguish contamination from irradiation and compare their hazards.
Describe uses of nuclear radiation for exploring internal organs and for controlling or destroying unwanted tissue.
Explain how ionising radiation harms human tissue.
Explain why hazards differ by the radiation emitted and the half-life.

topics.title: P5.3 How can radioactive materials be used to provide energy? (separate science only)

outcomes.text: Recall that unstable nuclei can split in nuclear fission.
Relate energy released in fission to ionising radiation and kinetic energy of the products.
Explain how fission can cause a chain reaction.
Describe nuclear fusion and that some mass is converted to radiation energy.

units.title: Chapter P6: Matter - models and explanations

topics.title: P6.1 How does energy transform matter?

outcomes.text: Define density and describe how to measure the density of solid and liquid objects.
Recall and apply density = mass / volume.
Describe the energy transfers when a system is changed by heating.
Define specific heat capacity and distinguish it from specific latent heat.
Apply change in internal energy = mass x specific heat capacity x temperature change, and explain how to measure heat capacity safely.

subtopics.title: Changes of state and energy calculations

outcomes.text: Apply energy for change of state = mass x specific latent heat.
Describe all the changes in how energy is stored when a system changes and its temperature rises.
Calculate energy transfers for temperature changes in mechanical, electrical and thermal processes.

topics.title: P6.2 How does the particle model explain the effects of heating?

outcomes.text: Explain differences in density between solids, liquids and gases in terms of particle arrangement.
Use the particle model to show mass is conserved in melting, freezing, evaporating, condensing and sublimating, and that these physical changes are reversible.
Use the particle model to describe how heating raises stored energy and temperature or changes state.
Explain how molecular motion in a gas relates to its temperature and pressure, including temperature and pressure at constant volume.

topics.title: P6.3 How does the particle model relate to material under stress?

outcomes.text: Explain with examples that stretching, bending or compressing an object needs more than one force.
Use the particle model to explain elastic and plastic deformation.
Describe the force-extension relationship for a spring and how to measure it.
Distinguish linear from non-linear force-extension relationships.
Recall and apply force = spring constant x extension for linear systems.
Calculate the work done stretching a spring from the area on a force-extension graph, and describe measuring it safely.
Apply energy stored = half x spring constant x extension squared.

topics.title: P6.4 How does the particle model relate to pressures in fluids? (separate science only)

outcomes.text: Recall that fluid pressure causes a force normal to any surface.
Recall and apply pressure = force / area.
Recall that gases can be compressed or expanded by pressure changes, producing a net force at right angles to any surface.
Use the particle model to explain why increasing a gas's volume at constant temperature lowers its pressure.
Apply pressure x volume = constant for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature.

subtopics.title: Pressure in liquids and the atmosphere

outcomes.text: Describe a simple model of the atmosphere and explain why atmospheric pressure falls with height.
Explain why pressure in a liquid varies with depth and density.
Apply pressure = density x gravitational field strength x depth.
Explain how pressure increase with depth causes an upward force on a submerged object.
Describe and explain the factors that decide whether an object floats or sinks.

topics.title: P6.5 How can scientific models help us understand the Big Bang? (separate science only)

outcomes.text: Recall the main features of the solar system and how planets, moons and artificial satellites are similar and different.
Explain how gravity changes a planet's velocity but not its speed in a circular orbit.
Explain that a stable orbit's radius must change if its speed changes.
Recall that the solar system formed from dust and gas drawn together by gravity.
Use the particle model to explain how doing work on a gas raises its temperature.
Explain how the Sun formed and reached equilibrium between gravitational collapse and fusion energy.
Explain the red-shift of light from receding galaxies.
Explain how the link between a galaxy's distance and speed is evidence for an expanding universe.
Explain how evidence of an expanding universe leads to the Big Bang model.

topics.title: IaS1 What needs to be considered when investigating a phenomenon scientifically?

outcomes.text: Use scientific theories and tentative explanations to develop and justify hypotheses and predictions.
Suggest apparatus, materials and techniques, justified by precision, accuracy and validity.
Recognise the importance of scientific quantities and how they are determined.
Identify factors to control and how to control them.
Suggest and justify a sample size or range of values to measure.
Plan clear, logically sequenced experiments to make observations, test hypotheses, collect data or explore phenomena.
Identify hazards and suggest ways to minimise risk.
Use scientific vocabulary and diagrammatic, graphical, numerical and symbolic forms to explain the rationale and methods.

topics.title: IaS2 What processes are needed to draw conclusions from data?

outcomes.text: Present observations and data in suitable formats.
Use SI units, prefixes and powers of ten, and interconvert units.
Translate data from one form to another.
Use an appropriate number of significant figures.
Choose graph types, axes and scales, plot points, draw a line of best fit and show uncertainty.
Identify patterns and trends, use range and mean, and read gradients, interpolation and extrapolation from graphs.
Evaluate data for accuracy, precision, repeatability and reproducibility, identify random and systematic error, and decide whether to discard an outlier.
Evaluate an experimental strategy, suggest improvements and further investigations.
Interpret data to make inferences and reasoned conclusions using scientific vocabulary.
Explain how far data increase or decrease confidence in a prediction or hypothesis.

topics.title: IaS3 How are scientific explanations developed?

outcomes.text: Identify a correlation in text, tables or graphs and distinguish a correlation from a cause-effect link.
Suggest factors that raise the chance of an outcome without always causing it.
Explain why individual cases are not convincing evidence for or against a correlation.
Use the presence or absence of a plausible mechanism to accept or reject a causal claim.
Describe and explain examples of scientific theories that changed when new evidence arrived.
Describe in outline the peer review process.
Use representational, spatial, descriptive, computational and mathematical models to solve problems, make predictions, develop explanations and identify limitations.

topics.title: IaS4 How do science and technology impact society?

outcomes.text: Describe everyday technological applications of science that made significant positive differences to lives.
Identify risks that arose from new scientific or technological advances.
For a situation, identify risks and benefits to those involved, discuss a course of action, explain willingness to accept risk and tell perceived from calculated risk.
Explain why different decisions on the same issue may suit different personal, social, economic or environmental contexts.
Distinguish questions science can answer from those it cannot, and state ethical issues and different views clearly.
Explain why scientists should communicate their work to a range of audiences.
